3.  **Heights of adults.** Researchers studying anthropometry collected body measurements, as well as age, weight, height and gender, for 507 physically active adults.
Summary statistics for the distribution of heights (measured in centimeters, cm), along with a histogram, are provided below.
[@Heinz:2003]

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-asp: 0.5
bdims |>
  summarise(
    Min    = round(min(hgt), 1),
    Q1     = round(quantile(hgt, 0.25), 1),
    Median = round(median(hgt), 1),
    Mean   = round(mean(hgt), 1),
    Q3     = round(quantile(hgt, 0.75), 1),
    Max    = round(max(hgt), 1),
    SD     = round(sd(hgt), 1),
    IQR    = round(IQR(hgt), 1)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Statistic",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  kbl(linesep = "", booktabs = TRUE, align = "lr", col.names = NULL) |>
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), 
    latex_options = "HOLD_position",
    full_width = FALSE
  )

ggplot(bdims, aes(x = hgt)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "Height (cm)", y = "Count")
```

a.  What are the point estimates for the average and median heights of active adults?

b.  What are the point estimates for the standard deviation and IQR of heights of active adults?

c.  Is a person who is 1m 80cm (180 cm) tall considered unusually tall?
    And is a person who is 1m 55cm (155cm) considered unusually short?
    Explain your reasoning.

d.  The researchers take another random sample of physically active adults.
    Would you expect the mean and the standard deviation of this new sample to be the ones given above?
    Explain your reasoning.

e.  The sample means obtained are point estimates for the mean height of all active individuals, if the sample of individuals is equivalent to a simple random sample.
    What measure do we use to quantify the variability of such an estimate?
    Compute this quantity using the data from the original sample under the condition that the data are a simple random sample.

\vfill

6.  **Heights of adults, bootstrap interval.** Researchers studying anthropometry collected body measurements, as well as age, weight, height and gender, for 507 physically active adults.
The histogram below shows the sample distribution of bootstrapped means from 1,000 different bootstrap samples.
[@Heinz:2003]

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.4
set.seed(47)
bdims |>
  specify(response = hgt) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, fill = IMSCOL["green", "full"]) +
  labs(
    x = "Bootstrapped mean of height (cm)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "1,000 bootstrap means"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(170, 172.4, 0.4),
    labels = label_comma(scale = 1, accuracy = 0.1)
  )
```

a.  Given the bootstrap sampling distribution for the sample mean, find an approximate value for the standard error of the mean.

b.  By looking at the bootstrap sampling distribution (1,000 bootstrap samples were taken), find an approximate 90% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the true average adult height in the population from which the data were randomly sampled.
    Provide the interval as well as a one-sentence interpretation of the interval.

c.  By looking at the bootstrap sampling distribution (1,000 bootstrap samples were taken), find an approximate 90% bootstrap SE confidence interval for the true average adult height in the population from which the data were randomly sampled.
    Provide the interval as well as a one-sentence interpretation of the interval.

\vfill
\clearpage

8.  **$t$-distribution.**
The figure below shows three unimodal and symmetric curves: the standard normal (z) distribution, the $t$-distribution with 5 degrees of freedom, and the $t$-distribution with 1 degree of freedom.
Determine which is which, and explain your reasoning.

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.4
#| fig-width: 5
x <- seq(-5, 5, 0.01)
z <- dnorm(x)
t1 <- dt(x, 5)
t5 <- dt(x, 1)

df <- tibble(
    xx = c(x, x, x),
    yy = c(z, t1, t5),
    curve = factor(c(rep("solid", length(x)), rep("dashed", length(x)), rep("dotted", length(x))), 
                   levels = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")),
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = xx, y = yy, color = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(size = 0.8) +
  scale_color_openintro("three") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-4, -2, 0, 2, 4)) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = c(0.8, 0.8),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank()
  )
```

9.  **Length of gestation, confidence interval.** Every year, the United States Department of Health and Human Services releases to the public a large dataset containing information on births recorded in the country.
This dataset has been of interest to medical researchers who are studying the relation between habits and practices of expectant mothers and the birth of their children.
In this exercise we work with a random sample of 1,000 cases from the dataset released in 2014.
The length of pregnancy, measured in weeks, is commonly referred to as gestation.
The histograms below show the distribution of lengths of gestation from the random sample of 1,000 births (on the left) and the distribution of bootstrapped means of gestation from 1,500 different bootstrap samples (on the right).

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-asp: 0.3
p_sample <- ggplot(births14, aes(x = weeks)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Gestation (weeks)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Random sample of 1,000 births"
  )

set.seed(47)
births14_boot <- births14 |>
  specify(response = weeks) |>
  generate(reps = 1500, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

p_boot <- ggplot(births14_boot, aes(x = stat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = IMSCOL["green", "full"]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(38.4, 38.5, 38.6, 38.7, 38.8, 38.9)) +
  labs(
    x = "Bootstrapped mean of gestation (weeks)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "1,500 bootstrap means"
  )

p_sample + p_boot
```

a.  Given the bootstrap sampling distribution for the sample mean, find an approximate value for the standard error of the mean.

b.  By looking at the bootstrap sampling distribution (1,500 bootstrap samples were taken), find an approximate 99% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the true average gestation length in the population from which the data were randomly sampled.
    Provide the interval as well as a one-sentence interpretation of the interval.

c.  By looking at the bootstrap sampling distribution (1,500 bootstrap samples were taken), find an approximate 99% bootstrap SE confidence interval for the true average gestation length in the population from which the data were randomly sampled.
    Provide the interval as well as a one-sentence interpretation of the interval.

16.  **Diamonds, bootstrap interval.** We have data on two random samples of diamonds: 23 0.99 carat diamonds and 23 1 carat diamonds.
Provided below is a histogram of bootstrap differences in means of price per carat of diamonds that weigh 0.99 carats and diamonds that weigh 1 carat.
[@ggplot2]

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.5
set.seed(47)
diamonds_100_99_sample <- diamonds |>
  filter(carat %in% c(1, 0.99)) |>
  group_by(carat) |>
  slice_sample(n = 23) |> 
  mutate(
    ppc   = price/carat/100,
    carat = if_else(carat == 1, paste(carat, "carat"), paste(carat, "carats"))
  )
    
diamonds_100_99_sample |>
  specify(ppc ~ carat) |>
  generate(1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("0.99 carats", "1 carat")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + 
  geom_histogram(fill = IMSCOL["green", "full"]) +
  labs(
    title = "1,000 bootstrapped differences in means",
    x = "Difference in bootstrapped means of price per carat\n(0.99 carats - 1 carat)", 
    y = "Count"
)
```

a.  Using the bootstrap distribution, create a (rough) 95% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the true population difference in prices per carat of diamonds that weigh 0.99 carats and 1 carat.

b.  Using the bootstrap distribution, create a (rough) 95% bootstrap SE confidence interval for the true population difference in prices per carat of diamonds that weigh 0.99 carats and 1 carat.
    Note that the standard error of the bootstrap distribution is 4.64.
\clearpage

19.  **Diamonds, mathematical interval.** We have data on two random samples of diamonds: one with diamonds that weigh 0.99 carats and one with diamonds that weigh 1 carat.
Each sample has 23 diamonds.
Sample statistics for the price per carat of diamonds in each sample are provided below.
Assuming that the conditions for conducting inference using a mathematical model are satisfied, construct a 95% confidence interval for the true population difference in prices per carat of diamonds that weigh 0.99 carats and 1 carat.
[@ggplot2]

```{r}
set.seed(47)
diamonds_100_99_sample <- diamonds |>
  filter(carat %in% c(1, 0.99)) |>
  group_by(carat) |>
  slice_sample(n = 23) |> 
  mutate(
    ppc   = price/carat/100,
    carat = if_else(carat == 1, paste(carat, "carat"), paste(carat, "carats"))
    )

diamonds_100_99_summary <- diamonds_100_99_sample |>
  group_by(carat) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = format(mean(ppc), digits = 4, nsmall = 2),
    SD = format(sd(ppc), digits = 4, nsmall = 2),
    n = n()
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Mean = paste0("$", Mean),
    SD = paste0("$", SD)
    )
    
diamonds_100_99_summary |>
  kbl(linesep = "", booktabs = TRUE, align = "lccc", col.names = c("", "Mean", "SD", "n"), digits = 2) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), 
                latex_options = "HOLD_position",
                full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1:4, width = "6em")
```

27.  **High School and Beyond, bootstrap interval.** We considered the differences between the reading and writing scores of a random sample of 200 students who took the High School and Beyond Survey.
The mean and standard deviation of the differences are $\bar{x}_{read-write} = -0.545$ and $s_{read-write}$ = 8.887 points.
The bootstrap distribution below was produced by bootstrapping from the sample of differences in reading and writing scores 1,000 times.

:::: {layout="[-0.05, 0.45, -0.05, 0.45]"}
:::{#question}
a.  Find an approximate 95% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the true average difference in scores (read - write).\

b.  Find an approximate 95% bootstrap SE confidence interval for the true average difference in scores (read - write).
:::
:::{#plot}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| out-width: 98%
set.seed(1234)
hsb2 |>
  mutate(diff = read - write) |>
  specify(response = diff) |>
  generate(1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, fill = IMSCOL["green", "full"]) +
  labs(
    title = "1,000 means of bootstrapped differences",
    x = "Mean of bootstrapped difference scores\n(read - write)", 
    y = "Count"
  )+
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```
:::
::::

c.  Interpret both confidence intervals using words like "population" and "score".

d.  From the confidence intervals calculated above, does it appear that there is a discernible difference in reading and writing scores, on average?

28.  **Global warming, bootstrap interval.** We considered the change in the 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature in 1950 versus 2022 at 26 sampled locations from the NOAA database.
[@webpage:noaa19482018] The mean and standard deviation of the reported differences are 2.53$^\circ$F and 2.95$^\circ$F.

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.4
set.seed(1234)
us_temperature |>
  group_by(station, year) |>
  summarize(temp_90 = quantile(tmax, probs = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = station, names_from = year, values_from = temp_90) |>
  mutate(diff = `2022` - `1950` ) |>
  specify(response = diff) |>
  generate(1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = IMSCOL["green", "full"]) +
  labs(
    title = "1,000 bootstrapped means of differences",
    x = "Mean of differences in score\n(Year 2022 - Year 1950)", 
    y = "Count"
  )
```

a.  Calculate a 90% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the average difference of 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature between 1950 and 2022.

b.  Calculate a 90% bootstrap SE confidence interval for the average difference of 90$^{th}$ percentile high temperature between 1950 and 2022.

c.  Interpret both intervals in context.

d.  Do the confidence intervals provide convincing evidence that there were hotter high temperatures in 2022 than in 1950 at NOAA stations?
    Explain your reasoning.

```{r}

  ~Year,        ~Mean, ~SD, ~n,
  "2009",       12,    3.5, 50,

  ) |>
  kbl(linesep = "", booktabs = TRUE, align = "lccc") |>

    full_width = FALSE
  ) |>
```
